strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark: FT-Dojo is the first interactive environment for end-to-end LLM fine-tuning with joint data curation and training configuration optimization, addressing a clear gap beyond fixed-data benchmarks like MLE-Bench

Comprehensive evaluation: 13 diverse tasks across 5 domains with proper train/val/test separation, multiple baseline types (base model, human expert, general-purpose agent), and systematic ablations on data scale, backbone LLM, and model size

Well-articulated problem analysis: Three key challenges (context management, inefficient exploration, limited feedback understanding) clearly motivated and directly address observed limitations of general-purpose agents

Honest treatment of limitations: Candid discussion of emergent capabilities (cross-domain transfer in Table QA/Chemistry) and fundamental gaps (planning myopia, causal reasoning limitations) strengthens credibility
Reproducibility focus: Extensive appendices providing data sources, implementation details, complete results, case studies, and modular architecture design facilitating future extensions
Practical system design: FT-Agent's three-stage architecture (strategy proposal, fail-fast validation, structured feedback analysis) addresses real engineering challenges in autonomous fine-tuning
weaknesses: Weak statistical rigor: No significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis across runs. Performance differences (e.g., Finance 67.53% vs 64.73%) could be within noise. Small test sets (15-300 samples) create high variance without error bars

Overclaimed results without sufficient evidence: AIME breakthrough (13.3% vs 0% on 15 test samples) framed as autonomous reasoning synthesis lacks robustness. Efficiency claims (24.37% vs 17.31% improvement rate) unvalidated statistically

Unfair baseline comparison: OpenHands heavily scaffolded via main.py structure (B.2.3) with fixed DataAgent→TrainAgent→EvalAgent pipeline, undermining the 'general-purpose vs specialized' framing. Human baseline restricted to Two-Pass protocol may underestimate capability

Limited novelty in agent design: FT-Agent mechanisms are sensible engineering (fail-fast validation, context management, feedback parsing) but not algorithmically novel. Core contribution is application to fine-tuning rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient ablation of core mechanisms: Missing critical analysis of which FT-Agent components (fail-fast validation, structured memory, feedback analysis) drive improvements. Current ablations test data/backbone/scale but not the agent design itself

Speculative causal reasoning claims: Pattern-matching vs causal reasoning distinction (Section 4.4, D.3) based on anecdotal PI4PC trajectory with hedging language. Mol_Edit example of RDKit discovery attributed to pattern-matching but actually represents effective problem-solving
Reproducibility limited by proprietary APIs: Dependence on GPT-5.2/GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini limits future reproducibility. No discussion of API stability, cost trajectory, or availability guarantees

Underexplored experimental choices: Why 2,000 max samples? Why 12-hour budget? Sensitivity analysis missing. Data scaling finding (Figure 3a, Visualization degradation with 5k samples) counterintuitive but inadequately analyzed
Limited generalization: Results only on FT-Dojo's 13 tasks. Unclear if insights transfer beyond this specific benchmark or to other fine-tuning domains (medical, legal, etc.)
Incomplete formal specification: Equation 1 presents joint optimization of θd and θt, but agent actually optimizes sequentially. Gap between theory and practice not addressed

strengths: Well-motivated and novel problem formulation: Clearly articulates why autonomous end-to-end LLM fine-tuning differs fundamentally from traditional ML engineering, addressing a genuine gap in literature
Comprehensive benchmark design: FT-Dojo comprises 13 well-designed tasks across 5 domains with rigorous data handling, modular architecture, and strict validation/test separation protocols
Thorough experimental evaluation: Controlled protocol with multiple baselines, 3-run statistics for FT-Agent, comprehensive ablations, and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility

Insightful case studies and honest limitations: Clear documentation of both emergent capabilities (cumulative learning, cross-domain transfer) and fundamental limitations (causal reasoning gap, planning myopia) with decision traces providing transparent evidence
Exceptional presentation: Well-structured writing, clear figures/tables, and comprehensive appendices facilitate understanding and reproducibility
Comprehensive technical documentation: Detailed prompt architecture (Appendix G), implementation details for all baselines (Appendix B), and dataset statistics enable thorough understanding
weaknesses: Statistical and methodological concerns: Small test sets on key tasks (AIME: 15 examples, Visualization: 25), unequal runs between FT-Agent (3) and baselines (1), substantial variance on some metrics (Reaction: ±11.22), and no significance testing limit confidence in quantitative conclusions

Baseline comparison fairness issues: OpenHands receives explicit scaffolding guidance, Manual SFT constrained to 'two-pass' protocol (undermined by Table 6 showing LLM-assisted variant achieving 20% on AIME vs. FT-Agent 13.33%), and comparisons only on single runs—raising questions about experimental validity

Limited algorithmic novelty: Three mechanisms (structured planning, fail-fast validation, feedback analysis) are domain-specific engineering heuristics rather than algorithmic innovations, hand-crafted rather than learned, with limited principled justification for why they work

Unresolved causal reasoning limitations: PI4PC case study (Table 9) demonstrates agents fail at causal diagnosis using hedging language ('likely,' 'appears'), cycling through generic techniques—fundamental limitation is identified but neither investigated nor addressed

Unclear practical applicability: Only one target model tested (Qwen2.5-7B), GPT-5.2 backbone is expensive/closed-source, no cost-benefit analysis vs. human engineers, ROI analysis absent, and generalization to messy real-world data (vs. clean benchmarks) unclear

Reproducibility and generalization limitations: Code URL appears truncated in manuscript, heavy dependence on closed-source APIs (GPT-5.2, GPT-5) prevents independent reproduction, test on single model limits generalization claims, and evaluation limited to artificial benchmark scenarios with held-out test sets

Incomplete mechanism analysis: Data construction evaluation conflates identifying missing components (e.g., CoT synthesis) with sophisticated engineering; cross-domain mixing strategies appear task-specific with unclear scalability; interaction between mechanisms not analyzed

Limited scope and comparisons: 13 tasks is moderate for a benchmark, missing comparisons with other recent code generation agents or ML automation systems, and chemical reaction prediction shows high variance limiting conclusions

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic study of autonomous end-to-end LLM fine-tuning with data strategy and training configuration as joint optimization targets

Well-designed interactive benchmark: FT-Dojo provides complete ecosystem (sandboxed execution, structured feedback, Meta API) rather than static datasets; proper data hygiene with strict train/val/test separation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple baselines (manual, OpenHands, frontier agents), controlled protocol with identical external resources, ablations on data scale/backbone/model scale
Pragmatic agent design: Three mechanisms (structured planning, fail-fast validation, feedback analysis) directly address real obstacles with demonstrated benefits (2.2× more effective iterations)
Transparent limitations analysis: Honest case studies revealing both emergent capabilities (cross-domain transfer) and fundamental deficits (causal reasoning, planning myopia) with concrete evidence
Strong reproducibility: Comprehensive appendices (A-G) with data sources, baseline implementations, full prompt architecture, clear experimental specifications
Valuable community insights: Demonstrates where autonomous fine-tuning helps (sparse supervision, structured tasks) vs. fails, useful for future research directions
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in agent mechanisms: Structured planning/fail-fast validation/feedback analysis represent well-executed engineering rather than algorithmic innovation; value lies in combination and domain application rather than new ideas

Heavy dependence on frontier models: FT-Agent with GPT-5.2 achieves 42.83% avg; drops to 35.83% with DeepSeek-V3.2 and 31.97% with Qwen3.5. Limited investigation into why frontier intelligence is necessary constrains generalizability and practical impact
Statistical asymmetry in comparisons: FT-Agent evaluated with 3 runs (mean±std); baselines with 1 run. Asymmetry weakens comparative claims despite budget constraints acknowledgment

Constrained experimental setup limits generalization: 12-hour wall-clock budget favors fail-fast approaches; single GPU type (B200); max 2k training samples are reasonable but limit generalizability of findings
Small evaluation sets reduce statistical power: AIME has only 15 val/15 test examples; several tasks have 25-50 test examples. Limits reliability of some conclusions despite proper data separation

Identified limitations not addressed with solutions: Causal reasoning gap (agents apply generic techniques without understanding roots), planning myopia, long-horizon planning acknowledged but not solved; Mol Edit success attributed to RDKit exposure rather than principled mechanisms

Manual baseline fairness questions: LLM-assisted variant (Table 6) matches or exceeds FT-Agent on several tasks (AIME: 20% vs 13.33%). Constrained two-pass protocol may not represent realistic comparison point
Limited cross-domain transfer analysis: While Figure 5 shows impressive cross-domain mixing, analysis of when/why agents choose this is limited; unclear if deliberate hypotheses or emergent behaviors
